report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister’s claim is supported for *prescription, purified cannabidiol* used **as an add-on** to existing antiseizure drugs in drug-resistant Dravet syndrome—not for over-the-counter CBD products.

The key double-blind randomized trial (120 patients, ages 2–18; 14 weeks) found cannabidiol 20 mg/kg/day reduced monthly convulsive seizures by a median **38.9%**, versus **13.3%** with placebo. More participants achieved at least a 50% reduction (43% vs 27%). It did not establish that most children become seizure-free, and seizure counts were caregiver-reported.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A second randomized dose-ranging trial (199 children) also found benefit: 10 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures **48.7%**, compared with **26.9%** on placebo; this supports a real treatment effect at a lower dose as well.  
https://z-lib.id/article/151618189

The evidence is bolstered by a systematic review/meta-analysis of four randomized trials (550 people with Dravet or Lennox-Gastaut syndromes), which assessed seizure reduction and adverse effects.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30390221/

**Important limits/harms:** Cannabidiol caused more adverse events than placebo—commonly sleepiness, diarrhea, reduced appetite, fatigue, and vomiting. It can elevate liver enzymes (especially with valproate) and interact with clobazam; monitoring and clinician-directed dosing are important. The FDA-approved product is Epidiolex, indicated for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients aged ≥1 year.  
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=8bf27097-4870-43fb-94f0-f3d0871d1eec&type=display
